subjects.name: Cells and Tissues
defs: Movement of substances across a membrane using energy from ATP.
Describing a molecule containing both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions.
The flexible phospholipid bilayer surrounding a cell that regulates passage of substances.
The movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration.
The process of a cell engulfing material by enveloping it in membrane.
The fuzzy carbohydrate coating surrounding a cell formed from glycoproteins.
A protein with carbohydrate molecules attached that extend into the extracellular space.
Describing a molecule or region that is attracted to water.
Describing a molecule or region that repels and is repelled by water.
A protein embedded within the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane.
The specific molecule that binds to and activates a receptor.
The diffusion of water through a semipermeable membrane down its concentration gradient.
A protein attached to the inner or outer surface of the cell membrane.
The endocytosis of large particles such as invading bacterial cells.
An amphipathic lipid with a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
A recognition protein that selectively binds a specific molecule outside the cell.
The membrane property that allows some substances to pass while blocking others.
An ATPase that transports sodium out of a cell while moving potassium into it.
The stage of mitosis when sister chromatids separate and move apart.
The ordered sequence of events through which a cell grows and divides.
A structure of DNA and protein carrying genetic information.
The division of the cytoplasm following nuclear division.
The phase of the cell cycle when the cell grows and replicates DNA.
The stage of mitosis when chromosomes align at the cell equator.
The division of a somatic cell nucleus into two identical nuclei.
The first stage of mitosis when chromosomes condense and spindles form.
The final stage of mitosis when new nuclei begin to form.
Tissue that binds and supports other tissues and organs.
The outer germ layer giving rise to skin and nervous tissue.
The inner germ layer lining airways and digestive tract.
Sheets of cells covering surfaces and lining cavities and passageways.
One of three embryonic cell lineages forming all tissues and organs.
The middle germ layer giving rise to connective, muscle, and circulatory tissues.
Excitable tissue that contracts to produce body movement.
Excitable tissue that propagates electrochemical signals as nerve impulses.
A structure formed by several tissue types working together as a unit.
A group of cells sharing a common embryonic origin and function.
The skin, a stratified squamous epithelial membrane resting on connective tissue.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A membrane composed of epithelium attached to connective tissue.
A gland that secretes its product through a duct to a surface.
An epithelial membrane lining cavities opening to the exterior.
An epithelial membrane lining closed body cavities and covering organs.
A connective tissue membrane lining freely movable joint cavities.
A thin layer of cells covering body surfaces, organs, or cavities.

subjects.name: Skeletal and Muscular Systems
defs: Dense osseous tissue that withstands compressive forces and forms the outer shell of bones.
Tubular shaft running between the proximal and distal ends of a long bone.
Sheet of hyaline cartilage in an immature bone's metaphysis that enables longitudinal growth.
Wide section at each end of a long bone, filled with spongy bone and red marrow.
Cell responsible for forming new bone by secreting uncalcified bone matrix.
Cell that breaks down and resorbs bone tissue during remodeling.
Mature bone cell that maintains the mineralized matrix and communicates through canaliculi.
Undifferentiated bone stem cell that divides and differentiates into osteoblasts.
Basic structural unit of compact bone, made of concentric layers of calcified matrix around a central canal.
Trabeculated osseous tissue that supports shifts in weight distribution inside bones.
Central vertical axis of the body, including the skull, vertebral column, and thoracic cage.
Seven vertebrae in the neck region that support the head and allow movement.
Small bone at the inferior end of the vertebral column formed by fused coccygeal vertebrae.
Portion of the skull that encloses and protects the brain.
Curved bones that form the sides of the thoracic cage and aid breathing.
Triangular bone formed by fused vertebrae at the base of the vertebral column.
Bony structure of the head that protects the brain and supports the face.
Flat bone in the center of the chest that articulates with most ribs.
Bony enclosure formed by the sternum, ribs, and thoracic vertebrae that protects thoracic organs.
Series of vertebrae extending from skull to pelvis that protects the spinal cord.
All bones of the upper and lower limbs plus the girdles attaching them to the axial skeleton.
Collarbone that articulates with the sternum medially and the scapula laterally.
Hip bone formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis.
Thigh bone; the longest and strongest bone in the body.
Thin lateral leg bone that stabilizes the ankle but does not bear weight.
Single bone of the upper arm, articulating with the scapula and forearm bones.
Lateral forearm bone that articulates with the humerus and carpal bones.
Shoulder blade that articulates with the humerus and clavicle.
Large medial leg bone that bears body weight and articulates with the femur and talus.
Medial forearm bone whose trochlear notch articulates with the humerus.
Striated involuntary muscle of the heart joined by intercalated discs.
Outer connective tissue layer surrounding an entire skeletal muscle.
Bundle of muscle fibers surrounded by perimysium within a skeletal muscle.
A motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates.
Long cylindrical organelle within a muscle fiber that contains sarcomeres.
Synapse between a motor neuron axon terminal and a muscle fiber membrane.
Repeating contractile unit of striated muscle containing actin and myosin filaments.
Striated, multinucleated muscle attached to bones that produces voluntary movement.
Non-striated involuntary muscle in walls of hollow organs and vessels.
Dense connective tissue that attaches a muscle to a bone.
Protein forming the thin myofilaments that slide during muscle contraction.
Muscle contraction that shortens the muscle to move a load.
Muscle contraction that lengthens the muscle as tension diminishes.
Sequence linking motor neuron signaling to contraction of a muscle fiber's sarcomeres.
Muscle contraction producing tension without change in muscle length.
Muscle contraction involving a change in muscle length under constant tension.
Region of muscle fiber sarcolemma at the neuromuscular junction with acetylcholine receptors.
Protein forming thick filaments whose heads pull actin during contraction.
Action of myosin pulling actin inward toward the M line.
Increase in the number of motor units activated to raise contraction strength.

subjects.name: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Systems
defs: A relay station that delays the electrical signal between the atria and ventricles.
An upper chamber of the heart that receives blood returning to the heart.
The sequence of contraction and relaxation events in the heart during one heartbeat.
The volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart muscle relaxes and fills with blood.
The outermost layer of the heart wall, also called the visceral pericardium.
A muscular organ that pumps blood through the body's blood vessels.
The thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall that contracts to pump blood.
The heart's natural pacemaker, located in the right atrium, that initiates each heartbeat.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood.
A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out to the lungs or body.
The largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
A small branch of an artery that leads into capillary beds.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart, usually oxygenated.
The force exerted by circulating blood on the walls of blood vessels.
The smallest blood vessel, where exchange of gases and nutrients occurs.
The simple squamous epithelium lining the interior of blood vessels.
The outermost layer of a blood vessel wall made of connective tissue.
The innermost layer of a blood vessel wall, lined by endothelium.
The middle layer of a blood vessel wall containing smooth muscle and elastic fibers.
A blood vessel that returns blood toward the heart, usually deoxygenated.
A large vein returning deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
A small vessel that collects blood from capillaries and feeds into veins.
A system classifying blood by antigens present on red blood cell surfaces.
A red blood cell that transports oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood.
The production of new red blood cells in the bone marrow.
The percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen.
The process that stops bleeding through vascular spasm, platelet plug, and clotting.
A white blood cell involved in immune defense against infection.
A white blood cell that mediates adaptive immunity, such as B and T cells.
The most abundant white blood cell, which phagocytizes bacteria and debris.
The liquid component of blood that carries cells, nutrients, and wastes.
A cell fragment that participates in blood clotting and hemostasis.
A tiny air sac in the lung where gas exchange with blood occurs.
A small airway branch within the lung that lacks cartilage support.
One of two main branches from the trachea leading into each lung.
The dome-shaped muscle that contracts to increase thoracic volume during inspiration.
A flap that closes the larynx during swallowing to prevent food aspiration.
The voice box containing vocal cords, located between the pharynx and trachea.
A slippery secretion that traps dust and pathogens in the respiratory tract.
The air-filled space behind the nose that warms, moistens, and filters air.
A muscular tube that connects the nasal cavity to the larynx and esophagus.
The serous membrane that lines the thoracic cavity and covers the lungs.
The windpipe, a tube reinforced with cartilage rings that conducts air to bronchi.
A waste gas produced by cells and removed by the lungs during exhalation.
The passive movement of gases from high to low concentration across membranes.
Gas exchange between the lungs and the blood across the respiratory membrane.
The percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen.
Gas exchange between the blood and body tissues at the cellular level.
A gas essential for cellular respiration, transported mainly by hemoglobin.
The pressure contributed by one gas in a mixture of gases.
The thin barrier between alveolar air and capillary blood for gas exchange.
A substance that reduces surface tension in alveoli to prevent collapse.
The mechanical process of moving air into and out of the lungs.

subjects.name: Nervous and Endocrine Systems
defs: A rapid change in membrane voltage that transmits an electrical signal.
The single fiber carrying an electrical signal away from the neuron cell body.
Branchlike fibers that receive incoming signals from other neurons or sensory cells.
A supportive neural tissue cell that maintains and supports neurons.
A lipid-rich insulating sheath around axons that speeds electrical signal conduction.
A cord-like bundle of axons in the peripheral nervous system transmitting signals.
A nerve cell that generates and propagates electrical signals throughout the nervous system.
A chemical messenger released from a neuron to alter a target cell.
A peripheral nervous system glial cell that forms myelin around axons.
The narrow junction where a chemical signal passes between neurons or cells.
The brain region including midbrain, pons, and medulla connecting brain to cord.
The brain region that compares movement commands with sensory feedback for coordination.
The outer gray matter of the brain where conscious perception occurs.
The brain region responsible for higher functions like memory, emotion, and consciousness.
The large white matter tract connecting the right and left cerebral hemispheres.
One of twelve nerves connected to the brain serving head and neck.
A diencephalon region coordinating autonomic and endocrine control of homeostasis.
Protective connective tissue coverings surrounding the central nervous system.
The central nervous system organ within the vertebral cavity mediating reflexes.
A diencephalon region relaying information between the cerebrum and periphery.
Six skeletal muscles controlling eye movement within the orbit.
The general sensory perception of movement of the body.
The special sense of smell with a direct connection to the cerebrum.
The second cranial nerve responsible for visual sensation.
Sensory perception of body position and movement of body parts.
General body senses including touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception.
A sensory receptor that transduces temperature stimuli into neural signals.
The eighth cranial nerve responsible for hearing and balance sensations.
The outer adrenal region producing mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids.
Endocrine glands atop each kidney regulating stress response and electrolytes.
The inner adrenal layer producing epinephrine and norepinephrine for stress.
An organ with endocrine and exocrine functions regulating digestion and glucose.
Small glands embedded in the thyroid that produce parathyroid hormone.
An endocrine gland secreting melatonin to regulate the sleep-wake cycle.
A bean-sized organ suspended from the hypothalamus that secretes hormones.
An organ involved in T-cell development, active during infancy and childhood.
A large endocrine gland responsible for synthesizing thyroid hormones.
A hormone stimulating sodium and fluid retention, increasing blood volume.
A hypothalamic hormone signaling kidneys to reabsorb water.
A thyroid hormone that decreases blood calcium levels.
A glucocorticoid important in glucose metabolism and immune downregulation.
The primary catecholamine secreted by the adrenal medulla during stress.
Female sex hormones important for reproductive tract development and pregnancy.
A pancreatic hormone stimulating glycogen breakdown, increasing blood glucose.
An anterior pituitary hormone promoting tissue building and nutrient metabolism.
A secretion traveling via blood or lymph to induce target cell responses.
A pancreatic hormone enhancing cellular glucose uptake, lowering blood glucose.
A hypothalamic hormone stimulating uterine contractions and milk ejection.
A steroid hormone important for sperm maturation and secondary sex traits.
An amino acid-derived thyroid hormone more abundant but less potent.

subjects.name: Digestive and Urinary Systems
defs: The passage of digested nutrients from the intestinal lumen through mucosal cells into blood or lymph.
The continuous muscular tube of the digestive tract that extends from the mouth to the anus.
A mass of chewed food ready to be swallowed.
The enzymatic breakdown of food molecules into smaller absorbable components.
The soupy liquid formed when food is mixed with digestive juices in the stomach.
The elimination of undigested material from the body in the form of feces.
The process of taking food into the gastrointestinal tract through the mouth.
Chewing, mixing, and segmentation that physically break food into smaller pieces for chemical digestion.
Wavelike muscular contractions and relaxations that propel food along the gastrointestinal tract.
The voluntary act of swallowing and the involuntary process of peristalsis that move food through the digestive tract.
Alternating contractions and relaxations of nonadjacent intestinal segments that mix food with digestive juices.
The section of the alimentary canal where most digestion and nutrient absorption occur.
Organs that aid digestion but are not part of the alimentary canal, such as the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
An alkaline fluid produced by the liver that emulsifies lipids for digestion.
An accessory organ that stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver.
The major functional cell of the liver that performs metabolic and secretory tasks.
The body's largest gland, whose main digestive role is producing bile.
An accessory organ that secretes pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.
An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that completes carbohydrate digestion in the small intestine.
The secretion of the pancreas containing digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.
An aqueous solution of proteins and ions secreted into the mouth by salivary glands.
A digestive enzyme in saliva that begins the chemical breakdown of starch.
An exocrine gland that secretes saliva into the mouth.
A cup-shaped sac surrounding the glomerulus that collects the filtrate.
Cup-like structures that receive urine from collecting ducts and pass it to the renal pelvis.
A tube that receives urine from nephrons and carries it toward the renal pelvis.
The smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts to expel urine.
The nephron segment that receives filtrate from the loop of Henle and empties into collecting ducts.
A tuft of capillaries in the kidney that filters blood based on size.
The descending and ascending portion of a nephron between the proximal and distal tubules.
The functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine.
The highly active nephron segment that reabsorbs and secretes substances from filtrate.
The part of a nephron consisting of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
The tube that transports urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body.
A hormone that increases water reabsorption from the kidney's collecting tubules.
A state in which the body contains insufficient water in blood and tissues.
The production of an abnormally large volume of urine.
Fluid located outside cells, including interstitial fluid, blood plasma, and other body fluids.
The fluid in small spaces between cells that is not contained within blood vessels.
The fluid contained within the cytosol of body cells.
A condition in which a deficiency of bicarbonate makes the blood overly acidic.
A condition in which an excess of bicarbonate makes the blood overly alkaline.
The concentration of solute particles per kilogram of blood plasma solvent, reflecting hydration status.
A condition in which excess carbon dioxide makes the blood overly acidic.
A condition in which a deficiency of carbon dioxide makes the blood overly alkaline.

subjects.name: Homeostasis
defs: The component that compares a monitored value to its normal range and activates an effector if needed.
The component that produces a change reversing a deviation and restoring the value to its normal range.
A cycle of stimulus, sensor, control center, and effector that regulates a physiological condition.
The process by which cells throughout the body maintain internal conditions within a narrow life-compatible range.
A mechanism that reverses a deviation from the set point, maintaining body parameters within normal range.
The restricted set of values for a physiological parameter that is optimally healthful and stable.
A mechanism that intensifies a change, moving the body farther from the normal range until an endpoint.
A component of a feedback system that monitors a physiological value and reports it to the control center.
The physiological value around which the normal range of a parameter fluctuates.
A deviation of a physiological parameter beyond its normal range that triggers a feedback response.
Hormone that breaks down glycogen to glucose, increasing metabolism and heat production.
Brain cells activated by cold that reduce skin blood flow and trigger heat-producing responses.
A cluster of brain cells stimulated when body temperature exceeds its normal range to promote cooling.
Involuntary skeletal muscle contractions that generate heat during severe cold exposure.
Activation of sweat glands whose evaporating sweat removes heat from the skin surface.
The brain region that receives temperature data and activates heat-loss or heat-gain responses.
The process of maintaining body temperature within its normal range through heat gain or loss.
Hormone released to increase metabolic activity and heat production throughout the body.
Narrowing of skin blood vessels that reduces blood flow to the surface to conserve heat.
Widening of skin blood vessels that increases blood flow to the surface to radiate heat.
A substance that donates hydrogen ions, lowering pH and increasing acidity.
A condition in which blood pH falls below 7.35, making it too acidic.
A condition in which blood pH rises above 7.45, making it too alkaline.
A substance that accepts hydrogen ions or donates hydroxyl ions, raising pH.
An ion that serves as a key buffer component and helps maintain acid-base balance.
The primary buffering system of interstitial fluid, maintaining a 20:1 bicarbonate to carbonic acid ratio.
A chemical system that prevents radical pH change by absorbing excess hydrogen or hydroxyl ions.
A weak acid formed from carbon dioxide and water that participates in buffering.
An enzyme in red blood cells that converts carbon dioxide into bicarbonate.
A measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution based on hydrogen ion concentration.
Hormone that increases sodium reabsorption in kidney tubules, with water following.
Hormone that increases water reabsorption from kidney collecting tubules.
A water channel protein inserted into kidney tubule membranes to increase water reabsorption.
A net loss of water resulting in insufficient water in blood and other tissues.
Production of urine in excess of normal levels, expelling excess body water.
The concentration of solute particles per kilogram of solvent, reflecting hydration state.
A sensory receptor in the hypothalamus that monitors blood osmolality.
The diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water concentration.
The solute-to-water ratio of blood plasma, monitored to assess hydration.
Physiological processes triggered by dehydration that produce conscious thirst and water-seeking.
